title: Joining three or more tables
objective: Chain joins across the whole warehouse (customers → orders → order_items → products → suppliers, returns), choosing the right join type at every step, and avoid fan-out and accidental INNER-ing of outer joins.
context: Real questions cross the whole model: revenue by category, refunds by supplier, customer value. Each extra join is another chance to drop or multiply rows, so the finance team wants every multi-table query reconciled against a known total.

exercises.title: Gross revenue by category
exercises.question: The CFO wants gross revenue by product category.
exercises.prompt: Return category, order_lines (number of order lines counted) and gross_revenue rounded to 2 decimals, one row per category (NULL category is its own group). Gross revenue = SUM(quantity * unit_price) over the order_items of VALID orders, i.e. orders with order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned') (cancelled and pending are excluded).
hints: Status lives in orders, money in order_items, category in products — three tables, two keys.
orders JOIN order_items ON order_id, then JOIN products ON product_id; filter valid statuses in WHERE.
FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id JOIN products p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id WHERE o.order_status IN (...) GROUP BY p.category
exercises.why: Revenue-by-dimension is the most common shape of a finance query. Reconcile: the categories must sum to the total.

recall.q: Which join in this chain multiplies rows and which does not?
recall.a: orders → order_items multiplies (one-to-many); order_items → products is a lookup (many-to-one) and does not.

exercises.join_notes: orders (60) → order_items: 150 rows (one-to-many; order 60 has no lines and drops). → products: still 150 (each line has exactly one product). WHERE keeps the 134 lines of the 53 valid orders. Grouped: 6 rows, summing to 13,035.69. The NULL category (product 20 'Mystery Gift Box', 13 lines, 503.75) comes from the products data, not from the join. INNER is safe: every line has an order and a product (order 31's lines are included — we never joined customers).

exercises.title: Line detail for the latest orders
exercises.question: Customer service wants a readable list of every line in orders placed from 2025-11-01 onward.
exercises.prompt: For orders with order_date >= '2025-11-01' (any status), return order_id, order_date, customer_name, product_name, quantity and line_total (quantity * unit_price) — one row per order line.
hints: Driving table: orders (filtered by date). Three lookups/expansions hang off it.
customers on customer_id, order_items on order_id, products on product_id.
FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON ... JOIN order_items oi ON ... JOIN products p ON ... WHERE o.order_date >= '2025-11-01'
exercises.why: Four-table detail queries power order-status pages and support tools; each join must be justified.

recall.q: Order 60 is dated 2025-12-27. Why is it missing?
recall.a: It has no order_items; the INNER JOIN to order_items drops it.

exercises.join_notes: 5 orders are dated on/after 2025-11-01 (56, 57, 58, 59, 60). Joining customers keeps all 5 (all have real customers). Joining order_items expands to 12 rows (3 + 2 + 5 + 2 + 0 lines) — order 60 (pending, no lines) drops out silently. products is a lookup, so the result stays 12 rows; order 58's customer name repeats 5 times.

exercises.title: Customer value: orders and revenue (avoid fan-out)
exercises.question: Account management wants each customer's number of valid orders and gross revenue.
exercises.prompt: Return customer_id, name, valid_orders (number of DISTINCT valid orders) and gross_revenue rounded to 2 decimals, for customers in the customers table who have at least one valid order with items. Gross revenue = SUM(quantity * unit_price) over the order_items of VALID orders, i.e. orders with order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned') (cancelled and pending are excluded).
hints: After joining order_items you're at LINE grain — each order appears once per line.
COUNT(o.order_id) would count lines; you need COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id).

SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS valid_orders, ROUND(SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price), 2) AS gross_revenue FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON ... JOIN order_items oi ON ... WHERE ... GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name
exercises.why: Fan-out is the most common silent error in multi-table SQL: counts of the 'one' side get inflated by the 'many' side.

recall.q: Customer 1 has 8 valid orders and 17 lines. What does COUNT(o.order_id) return after joining order_items?
recall.a: 17 — one per line. COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) returns 8.

exercises.join_notes: customers 20 → orders: 59 rows (order 31 is orphaned) → order_items: 148 rows; WHERE keeps 132 valid lines from 52 valid orders. Grouped: 16 customers. Fan-out example: customer 1 has 8 valid orders but 17 lines — plain COUNT would say 17. Missing: customers 18–20 (no orders), customer 16 (only a cancelled order) and the 363.30 of order 31, so the customers sum to 12,672.39 instead of the 13,035.69 total.

exercises.title: Return details across five tables
exercises.question: Quality wants every return with who bought it, what it was and which supplier made it — no return may be dropped.
exercises.prompt: Return return_id, return_date, customer_name, product_name, supplier_name and refund_amount for all 10 returns. customer_name / supplier_name are NULL when the customer / supplier is missing.
hints: Drive from returns; every hop is a parent lookup, so the row count can only stay at 10 or shrink.
Which lookups can fail? Check products 21/22 (no valid supplier). Use LEFT JOIN where a match may be missing.
FROM returns r JOIN order_items oi ON ... JOIN orders o ON ... LEFT JOIN customers c ON ... JOIN products p ON ... LEFT JOIN suppliers s ON s.supplier_id = p.supplier_id
exercises.why: When the driving table must fully survive, any lookup that can fail must be a LEFT JOIN — one stray INNER JOIN at the end of a chain quietly deletes rows.

recall.q: How many returns would you get with INNER JOIN suppliers, and why?
recall.a: 8 — returns 3 (product 22, NULL supplier) and 10 (product 21, supplier 9 missing) would be dropped.

exercises.join_notes: returns 10 rows. Every hop looks up a parent by its primary key, so nothing multiplies: 10 rows all the way. order_items, orders and products always match. customers also always matches here (no return is on order 31), so its LEFT JOIN is just a safety net. suppliers does NOT: return 3 (product 22 'Phone Stand', NULL supplier_id) and return 10 (product 21 'Water Bottle', supplier 9) get supplier_name NULL. An INNER JOIN to suppliers would silently drop them and 27.00 of refunds.

exercises.title: Net revenue by category
exercises.question: Finance wants gross revenue, refunds and net revenue by category.
exercises.prompt: Return category, gross_revenue, refunds (SUM of returns.refund_amount; 0 when none) and net_revenue (gross_revenue - refunds), all rounded to 2 decimals, one row per category (NULL category is its own group). Gross revenue = SUM(quantity * unit_price) over the order_items of VALID orders, i.e. orders with order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned') (cancelled and pending are excluded). Refunds are matched to order lines via order_item_id.
hints: Most lines have no return — they must still count toward gross revenue → LEFT JOIN returns.
Each line has at most one return, so the LEFT JOIN cannot double-count line revenue. COALESCE the refunds.
... JOIN products p ON ... LEFT JOIN returns r ON r.order_item_id = oi.order_item_id WHERE ... GROUP BY p.category
exercises.why: Net revenue is the number finance actually reports. Getting the join type wrong on returns either wipes out gross revenue (INNER) or double-counts it (if returns could have several rows per line).

recall.q: What would INNER JOIN returns do to gross_revenue?
recall.a: It would keep only the 10 returned lines, so gross_revenue would be the revenue of returned lines only.

exercises.join_notes: orders → order_items → products gives 150 lines; WHERE keeps 134 valid lines. The LEFT JOIN to returns matches 10 of them and NULL-pads 124 — still 134 rows, because order_item_id is unique in returns (no multiplication). Totals: gross 13,035.69, refunds 690.80, net 12,344.89. The NULL category has no returns, so its refunds are 0 only thanks to COALESCE (otherwise net would be NULL). INNER JOIN returns would shrink gross to just the 10 returned lines.

exercises.title: Supplier scorecard (all suppliers, outer-joined chain)
exercises.question: Procurement wants a scorecard for ALL 5 suppliers: products listed, products actually sold, and revenue.
exercises.prompt: Return supplier_id, supplier_name, products_listed (distinct products referencing the supplier), products_sold (distinct products of that supplier with at least one line in a valid order) and gross_revenue rounded to 2 decimals (0 when none), for all 5 suppliers. Gross revenue = SUM(quantity * unit_price) over the order_items of VALID orders, i.e. orders with order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned') (cancelled and pending are excluded).
hints: Every supplier must survive, so every hop after suppliers must be a LEFT JOIN — and the status filter must sit in ON.
Lines of invalid orders still arrive (o.* NULL); count/sum them only WHEN o.order_id IS NOT NULL. Alternatively pre-aggregate valid revenue per product in a CTE and LEFT JOIN it.

FROM suppliers s LEFT JOIN products p ON ... LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON ... LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = oi.order_id AND o.order_status IN (...) ... COUNT(DISTINCT p.product_id), COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN o.order_id IS NOT NULL THEN p.product_id END), SUM(CASE WHEN o.order_id IS NOT NULL THEN ... END)
exercises.why: Scorecards must list every entity, including the ones with nothing to report. That forces an all-LEFT chain with filters in ON — the hardest join shape to get right, and the most common in real dashboards.

recall.q: Why can't the status filter go in WHERE here?
recall.a: Supplier 5 (no products) and lines of invalid orders have NULL o.order_status; WHERE would delete supplier 5 entirely.

exercises.join_notes: suppliers 5 → products: 24 rows (23 products + NULL row for supplier 5). → order_items: 144 rows (one-to-many: each product repeats once per line; never-sold products 23, 24, 25 keep one NULL-padded row each). → orders with the status filter in ON: still 144 rows, but 20 have NULL order columns: 16 lines of cancelled/pending orders rejected by the ON filter plus the 4 padded rows. Result: 5 suppliers; Andes Trading shows 0 / 0 / 0.00. Revenues sum to 12,840.69, not 13,035.69: the 195.00 of products 21 (supplier 9) and 22 (NULL supplier) belongs to no listed supplier — that's what 'driving from suppliers' means.

worked_example.question: Show the order lines of order 41 with customer name and product name.
worked_example.sql:
SELECT o.order_id,
       c.name         AS customer_name,
       p.product_name,
       oi.quantity,
       oi.unit_price
FROM orders AS o
JOIN customers   AS c  ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
JOIN order_items AS oi ON oi.order_id   = o.order_id
JOIN products    AS p  ON p.product_id  = oi.product_id
WHERE o.order_id = 41;
worked_example.explanation: Order 41 → 1 customer (lookup) → its lines (one-to-many) → 1 product per line (lookup). The row count equals the number of lines of order 41. Note product 21 'Water Bottle' appears even though its supplier is broken — we never joined suppliers.

recipe:
**The join recipe — do it in this order, every time, before typing SQL**

1. **Pick the driving table.** Which table's rows is the answer *about*? ("every customer…", "each order line…")
   That table goes first, after `FROM` — it is the **left table**.
2. **Name the right table(s) and the shared key.** What column links them? Is it PK → FK (one-to-many) or
   one-to-one? Which side is the "many" side?
3. **Ask: "must every row of the left table survive, even with no match?"**
   - no → `INNER JOIN` (unmatched rows silently disappear)
   - yes → `LEFT JOIN` (unmatched rows stay, right-side columns become NULL)
   - rows from *both* sides must survive → `FULL OUTER JOIN`
4. **Predict the row count before you run it.** Count the inputs (`SELECT COUNT(*) …`), think about
   matches per row (0, 1 or many), write your guess down — then run and compare. A surprise means
   you misunderstood the grain, the key or the data.

**Chaining joins: walk the key path, one hop at a time**

```
customers ─customer_id─ orders ─order_id─ order_items ─product_id─ products ─supplier_id─ suppliers
                                               └─order_item_id─ returns
```

1. Pick the driving table (the grain of your answer, or the table that must fully survive).
2. Add **one** table at a time along the key path. For each hop repeat the recipe: right table, key,
   "must rows survive?" → join type, **predicted row count after this hop**.
3. Grain check: joining down a one-to-many path (orders → order_items) multiplies rows; looking up a
   parent (order_items → products) does not. Measures from the 'one' side (counting orders) need
   `COUNT(DISTINCT ...)` once you are at line grain.
4. **Once a table is LEFT-joined, everything joined *to it* must be LEFT-joined too** (or filtered in ON) —
   a later INNER JOIN or a WHERE on it throws the NULL-padded rows away again.
5. If two child tables both hang off the same parent (e.g. lines and refunds), aggregate each first
   (CTE), then join the aggregates — otherwise they multiply each other.
6. Reconcile: compare your total with a known total (here: gross revenue of valid orders = 13,035.69).

```sql
SELECT p.category, ROUND(SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price), 2) AS gross_revenue
FROM   orders      AS o                                  -- hop 0: 60 rows
JOIN   order_items AS oi ON oi.order_id   = o.order_id   -- hop 1: 150 (one-to-many)
JOIN   products    AS p  ON p.product_id  = oi.product_id-- hop 2: still 150 (lookup)
WHERE  o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')  -- 134 lines
GROUP  BY p.category;
```
common_mistakes: Counting orders (or customers) at line grain without DISTINCT — fan-out inflates the count.
LEFT JOINing a table and then INNER JOINing (or WHERE-filtering) something hanging off it, which deletes the NULL-padded rows again.
Joining two different child tables of the same parent (e.g. order_items and returns-per-order) at detail level, multiplying each other — aggregate first.
Not reconciling against a known total (13,035.69 gross) — the fastest way to detect dropped or duplicated rows.
Joining products → suppliers with INNER JOIN in a revenue query and silently losing products 21 and 22's revenue.
recall: What is the key path from customers to suppliers?
customers.customer_id → orders.customer_id; orders.order_id → order_items.order_id; order_items.product_id → products.product_id; products.supplier_id → suppliers.supplier_id.
In a chain, once a table is LEFT-joined, how must tables joined to it be joined?
Also LEFT (with filters in ON); an INNER join or WHERE on them removes the NULL-padded rows.
Parent → child hops (one-to-many), e.g. orders → order_items. Child → parent lookups do not.
How do you combine two independent one-to-many children safely?
Aggregate each to the parent's grain first (CTEs), then join the aggregates.
